summary: Specifies conventions for how S/MIME version 3.2 agents use X.509 certificates, including validating certificates and processing the information in them. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 8550.

plainLanguage.summary: Secure email needs digital ID cards. This document says how mail programs should check and use them. It was replaced by RFC 8550.

questions: how does s/mime 3.2 use x.509 certificates
subtitle: How mail programs check and use digital ID certificates for secure email.

tldr.problem: S/MIME agents need to verify that the public keys they use for secure email are valid and trustworthy, but X.509 certificates require careful handling with specific rules.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC specifies conventions for how S/MIME mail programs MUST process X.509 certificates, including validation, revocation checking, and interpretation of certificate extensions according to PKIX standards.
tldr.outcome: RFC 5750 was replaced by RFC 8550, which updated the algorithm requirements and extended key usage rules for modern cryptography.

today: RFC 5750 is a Proposed Standard and has been obsoleted by RFC 8550, which updates the requirements for S/MIME v3.2. The newer RFC changed the algorithm requirements to align with modern cryptographic standards and is the current reference for S/MIME certificate handling.

sections.title: Certificate Handling Basics
sections.content:
S/MIME (Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions) is a standard for sending and receiving secure MIME messages. Before a mail program can use a public key from someone's certificate to sign, verify, or encrypt a message, it must first validate that the certificate is genuine and currently valid.

This RFC builds on RFC 5280, the Internet X.509 Public Key Infrastructure (PKIX) Certificate and CRL Profile, and adds specific requirements for S/MIME agents. S/MIME agents MUST follow both this document and RFC 5280 when handling certificates. The RFC obsoletes RFC 3850, which covered S/MIME v3.1.
sections.plainLanguage: Before using someone's digital ID, a mail program checks it is real and not revoked. This explains what rules the program must follow.

sections.title: Certificate Storage and Choice
sections.content:
S/MIME messages can carry multiple X.509 certificates of different types. Receiving agents MUST support both v1 and v3 X.509 certificates as profiled in RFC 5280. They SHOULD also support version 2 attribute certificates, which allow additional information to be bound to a subject's public key certificate.

Receiving agents MUST handle an arbitrary number of certificates in arbitrary order and of arbitrary relationships to each other. Sending agents SHOULD include at least one chain of certificates from the sender up to (but not including) a certification authority that the recipient may trust. This increases the likelihood that recipients can establish trust in the sender's public key even if they do not have a local copy of the sender's certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: Messages can contain several ID cards. The mail program must be able to handle them all and figure out which one belongs to the sender.

sections.title: Email Addresses and Distinguished Names
sections.content:
An end-entity certificate MAY contain an Internet mail address. The email address SHOULD appear in the subjectAltName extension rather than in the distinguished name itself. Receiving agents MUST recognize certificates with no email address at all, and may use alternative mechanisms such as an address book to associate an email address with such a certificate.

When a signature is verified, receiving agents MUST check that the email address in the message's From or Sender header matches an Internet mail address in the signer's certificate, if such addresses are present in the certificate. If this check fails, the receiving agent SHOULD provide explicit alternate processing to display the mismatch to the user, such as showing the certificate details or available addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID card says who owns the key. The mail program checks that the person sending the message matches who is on the ID card.

sections.title: Certificate Validation and Revocation
sections.content:
S/MIME agents MUST validate certificates according to RFC 5280 before using any public key for security services such as signature verification or encryption. Validation includes checking the certificate chain back to a trusted certification authority (CA) and checking that the certificate has not expired or been revoked.

When checking revocation status, agents MUST be capable of using Certificate Revocation Lists (CRLs) as specified in RFC 5280. Both v1 and v2 CRLs MUST be supported. Receiving agents SHOULD retrieve fresh CRL information every time a certificate is verified, though in some cases (such as offline verification) this may not be possible. If an agent cannot verify that a certificate has not been revoked, it SHOULD warn the user before accepting the message.

Agents MUST also handle weak cryptographic algorithms carefully. RSA and DSA keys of less than 1024 bits are considered cryptographically insecure and implementations that support them MUST warn the user. For certificate and CRL signature verification, RSA with SHA-256 is MUST support, while RSA with SHA-1 is SHOULD-support (but discouraged).
sections.plainLanguage: Before trusting an ID card, the program checks it belongs to a real authority, has not expired, and has not been revoked. It also watches out for weak protections.

sections.title: Signing Algorithms and Certificate Extensions
sections.content:
S/MIME agents MUST correctly handle five key certificate extensions: basic constraints (which identifies CA certificates), key usage (which restricts what the key can be used for), authority key identifier, subject key identifier, and subject alternative names. If a key usage extension is present, it MUST be marked as critical, and receiving agents MUST NOT accept a signature if the certificate lacks either the digitalSignature or nonRepudiation bit set in the key usage extension.

The extended key usage extension, when present, further restricts what the key can be used for. For email protection, S/MIME receiving agents MUST check that the extended key usage extension contains either the emailProtection OID or the anyExtendedKeyUsage OID. Other certificate extensions MAY be included but SHOULD NOT be marked critical unless the proper handling of that extension is deemed critical to correct interpretation of the certificate.
sections.plainLanguage: The ID card contains special marks that say what it can be used for. The mail program checks these marks match what it is trying to do.
